questions.q: What single problem lies behind most short-channel effects?
options: In a short channel the drain competes with the gate for control of the source-to-drain barrier
In a short channel the gate oxide becomes too thin and leaks current into the substrate
In a short channel there are too few electrons in the source to carry the current
In a short channel the wires that connect the transistors become too long
questions.explain: The gate should be the only electrode controlling the barrier between source and drain. In a short channel the drain competes with it; roll-off, DIBL, punchthrough and swing degradation are all symptoms of that.

questions.q: The drain's influence reaches into the channel over the 'natural length' λ. Which change is the strongest lever for shrinking λ?
options: Putting the gate on more sides of the channel (double gate, FinFET, gate-all-around)
Making the gate oxide slightly thinner while keeping a single gate on top
Raising the supply voltage so that the gate pulls harder on the channel
Making the source and drain regions deeper and more heavily doped
questions.explain: A thinner body and a thinner oxide shrink λ only as square roots. Adding gates changes the prefactor and is the strongest lever: that is why the industry moved to FinFETs and gate-all-around transistors.

questions.q: The graph shows the conduction-band barrier along the channel. The red curve is a short channel at high drain voltage. Why is its lower barrier a problem when the transistor should be off?
questions.alt: Conduction-band edge from source to drain: a long channel has a high, wide barrier; a short channel at low drain voltage a lower one; a short channel at high drain voltage a much lower barrier
options: More electrons from the source can get over the lower barrier, so the off-current rises
Fewer electrons from the source can get over the lower barrier, so the on-current falls
A lower barrier makes the gate oxide thinner, so the gate leaks current
A lower barrier traps electrons in the channel, so the transistor stays on
questions.explain: The barrier holds back the electrons in the source. When the drain lowers it (drain-induced barrier lowering, DIBL), many more electrons get over it, so the transistor leaks even when the gate says 'off'.

questions.q: Threshold-voltage roll-off means V_T falls as the gate gets shorter. Why is this a problem for chip makers?
options: V_T becomes very sensitive to gate length, so tiny printing variations give large spreads in V_T
A lower V_T always gives more on-current, so the short transistors overheat the chip
A lower V_T needs a thicker gate oxide, which slows the transistors down
V_T becomes harder to measure, so the chips cannot be tested before they are sold
questions.explain: A lower V_T can be compensated. The real problem is that V_T becomes a steep function of L, so a 1 nm variation in printed gate length becomes tens of mV of V_T spread across the chip.

options: The source and drain depletion regions merge below the surface, where the gate cannot reach, and the barrier vanishes
The gate oxide breaks down under a high field, and current flows from the gate into the channel
Electrons tunnel from the valence band to the conduction band near the drain under the gate edge
The pinch-off point moves towards the source, so the current keeps rising slowly with drain voltage
questions.explain: Punchthrough is the terminal case of lost control: the source and drain depletion regions meet below the surface, the barrier disappears where the gate cannot reach, and current rises almost uncontrollably with V_DS.

questions.q: The graph shows transfer curves of a planar transistor as its gate is shortened from 60 nm to 15 nm. Besides shifting left, the curves become less steep (the swing grows). Why?
questions.alt: Drain current on a log scale against gate voltage for gate lengths of 60, 30, 20 and 15 nm: the shorter the gate, the further left and the less steep the curve
options: The drain adds its own coupling to the channel, so the gate's share of control over the barrier falls
The gate oxide is made thicker as the gate gets shorter, so the gate couples more weakly
Short channels run hotter, so the carriers have more thermal energy to cross the barrier
Short channels have fewer electrons in the source, so the current rises more slowly
questions.explain: The drain acts like an extra capacitor on the channel, so the gate controls a smaller share of the barrier and the curves flatten: the swing rises from about 70 to about 125 mV per decade. With the leftward shift, the off-current at V_GS = 0 rises by over four decades.

questions.q: Channel-length modulation makes the current keep rising slowly beyond saturation. What causes it?
options: The pinch-off point moves towards the source as V_DS rises, so the effective channel gets shorter
The gate oxide gets thinner as V_DS rises, so the gate gains more control over the channel
The carriers get lighter as V_DS rises, so they move faster through the channel
The source gets hotter as V_DS rises, so it emits more electrons into the channel
questions.explain: Past saturation the pinch-off point moves towards the source, shortening the effective channel, so the current keeps rising. It mainly matters in analogue circuits, where it sets the intrinsic gain.

questions.q: Why is impact ionisation by hot carriers much less of a problem in today's logic transistors than it was around 1990?
options: With a supply of about 0.7 V, carriers cannot gain the roughly 1.5 eV needed to create an electron–hole pair
Today's transistors are so short that carriers never reach the drain, so they cannot heat up
High-k gate oxides absorb all the hot carriers before they can reach the drain
Today's transistors run at much lower temperatures, so the carriers are never hot
questions.explain: Making an electron–hole pair needs about 1.5 eV, which a carrier cannot gain from a 0.7 V supply. In 1990, at 5 V, it was a serious problem, and the lightly doped drain (LDD) was invented to deal with it.

questions.q: Why do FinFETs and nanosheet transistors use undoped channels?
options: A tiny channel holds only a handful of dopant atoms, and their random number and position would make V_T vary widely
Dopant atoms are too large to fit inside a channel only a few nanometres thick
Undoped silicon conducts heat better, which keeps the small transistors cool
Undoped channels are cheaper to make because they skip a lithography step
questions.explain: A 15 × 15 × 20 nm channel at 10¹⁸ cm⁻³ holds about five dopant atoms, not five million. Random dopant fluctuation then gives a large spread in V_T; removing the doping removes this source of variability.

questions.q: The pictures show four architectures, from planar bulk to the nanosheet. What do the successive steps have in common?
questions.alt: Cross-sections of planar bulk (1 gate), FD-SOI (1 gate, thin body on oxide), FinFET (3 gates) and nanosheet gate-all-around (4 gates)
options: Each leaves less silicon for the drain's field to reach and puts gate on more sides
Each makes the channel longer, so the gate has more area to control it
Each swaps silicon for a new material with lighter electrons
Each raises the supply voltage, so the gate pulls harder
questions.explain: Planar → FD-SOI → FinFET → nanosheet is one move repeated: cut the semiconductor volume the drain can reach through, and surround the channel with more gate. Together with thinner oxides, these levers took the minimum gate length from about 39 nm to about 10 nm.
